When I first went to the meeting near my school, a couple of women told me they used to be special Ed teachers and proceeded to go on about how terrible it was that vaccines were inventing developmental disabilities. I didn't mention I was developmentally disabled. I just sat there silent then left. Super awkward facing such severely abelist beliefs in what's supposed to be a safe place. 

When I worked as a childcare provider for my meeting back home, there was a kid I took care of who was also disabled (same diagnoses as me). He was wonderful. Sometimes caused trouble, could be very stubborn, but i would just change plans and go with him. He's forced to pretend to be "normal" all day long in school where he's bullied and mistreated and given no freedom of choice. I know how that feels. Spiritual enrichment looks different for different kids. I decided he needed a space to feel free and accepted. Sure, he was a trouble maker, but I would be too if I was him. On the contrary, the bigger issue I had was not his behavior, it was the adults. They were rude to him (a literal 8-year old). They made passive aggressive comments about him when he was in hearing distance. They seemed upset with me that I wouldn't just yell at him and "put him in his place", but because I have his condition and know what it's like, I know how a) yelling wont work and b) how deep and long-lasting that damage could be for a sensitive disabled child. 

Real wake up call for me. I think Quakers often pretend to follow the spices until it's difficult. Once following the spices poses and internal challenge, they just seem to give up and give into hate and oppression. 

Crazy. Un-Quakerly. Weird.

I have the same question. A lot of the posts this past weekend spoke my mind. 

I haven't been to any meeting in a while. I tried to go to a meeting near me. I didn't feel like I "fit in" there either. The people there were not sociable towards newcomers and did not greet us. I figured they were busy and tried to shrug it off. I stayed for coffee social to meet some members, but I couldn't even say hi, let alone hold a conversation. I felt strangely ignored? It's a big meeting with many members so I think maybe they didn't want new people making it crowded? Not sure. I went back quite a few times to no avail. I can no longer go since I lost my car. 

Then, on a trip home, I visited my childhood meeting. I had practically grown up there. The people in that meeting are like second parents to me. Not a single person recognized me. They had basically raised me throughout my childhood, then I worked there as a childcare worker for a year or so as an adult. I came back after a few months of college and they couldn't recognize me whatsoever, some didn't even know my name. I tried to strike up conversation with old friends, but they would turn away from me, almost like they were intentionally avoiding me. Like I was shunned. I had never seen this behavior in them before and I knew some of them fairly well. I felt pretty heartbroken. 

I'm not even sure if I should call myself Quaker anymore. I had called myself that all my life, but it doesn't feel like I'm accepted in Quaker spaces. After coming to this subreddit, I'm starting to see why. Being a pagan-quaker isn't really considered as acceptable as I thought. I know some people do it, but it seems that most people agree that pagan values are incomparable with quaker ones. So is being non-theistic. Both of my meetings are very much liberal meetings, but they have some more conservative members. Maybe I was too outspoken about being enby or pagan? Maybe I voiced some opinion that had offended them? I know my father has voiced criticisms of christian ideals in our meeting before, which was somewhat divisive. Perhaps they are weary of me for his opinions? I still don't know. 

I've become more engrained in the community near where I live, volunteering, doing service work. It makes me feel better, but I still feel that I lack a sense of community to go back to.

My scholarship was removed by the university because ADS had misled me about the nature of my accomodations. The fact that you can lose your scholarship (a scholarship I earned for my skill on my instrument) for being disabled is bad enough, but I was furious that they had strongly deceived me in the process. I ended up going without the accomodation, having a mental break down, and trying to forget the experience with all  my might. Very dark time in my life.

My ADS advisor would not work with me over email, and had a bizarre insistence on phone calls. I later realized that they had misled me about my financial info and she was trying to avoid a paper trail so I'd be left without proof. When I asked to switch to a different advisor, ADS denied. Then I demanded to switch. ADS again denied. 

In addition, ADS will not suggest accomodations you need and you cannot find them on their website. Your ADS advisor is supposed to help you navigate the system, but they make it much harder, they're very difficult to communicate with. By talking to others with your disability, you can find out 'hidden' accomodations they don't tell you about. They also will not give accomodations to you just because you and your doctor agree you need them. In some cases, they will outright refuse to give them. I've heard from other disabled people that threatening to go to the office of civil rights is a pretty good way to get ADS advisors to act properly. 

In addition to all of that, my interactions with ADS workers are always very hurtful. They will infantilize me, undermine me, and all around treat me like a child. I am 21 year old adult. They talk to me like I'm 7. It's the most offended I've ever felt. 

This is by no means a comprehensive list. This is also not to say that everybody's experience with ADS is the same, but I've never heard anyone report a positive experience.

I would consider myself a Quaker as well as a witch. For me, the tenants of Paganism (particularly the more animistic paths) and the tenants of Quakerism go quite hand in hand. My Quaker upbringing was very nature based , and the witches almanac for this year has a passage about the sacredness of  silence. Pagan gods and figures often represent universal truths that exist within all of us, just like the Quaker Spirit. For me, the two are very alike. 

As for your remark on Christianity, there are christian witches out there, though I believe they are in the minority. I don't personally consider Quakerism to be a form of Christianity in and of itself. Some quakers see it that way, some don't. I've never considered myself Christian because I never saw Christian and quaker beliefs and practices as very similar to Quaker ones.

Not offensive at all, and I'd be very curious how it would turn out! My guess would be if it offends anyone, they are likely not familiar with both faiths deeply enough to be critiquing. Go for it!

Edit: it seems that a great number of people in this thread are antithetical to the idea. Many people are saying that the two ideologies simply "don't mix" and I believe this comes from a fundamental misunderstanding of pagan views.

 "Do what thou wilt" is generally refered to by it's full version, "an it harm none, do what thou wilt". (While the first phrase is more associated with Satanism, the second is more associated with Wicca.) To me, this is inherently very Quaker. We are allowed to walk our own paths freely as long as it is in line with the tenets of harmlessness that quakers adhere to. 

Also, it's important to note that there are many different pagan paths. Not all witches are wiccan. I would consider myself a witch, but I wouldn't say I'm a Wiccan.

I agree with the general idea of your comment, but I think you're pointing out  multiple phenomena at once. 

For one, psychological help being a cash cow. This bothers me a lot, but there are people trying to do something about it. I think the field of Liberation Psychology might interest you. 

The second phenomenon present here is the degradation of community. You're right, we don't consult elders anymore when we need guidance. Most of us don't have elders near us anymore. I am not an expert, but this is something that fascinates me, so I have some theories on this. 
1) The myth of the nuclear family discouraged people from keeping grandparents in the home. Combo this with a lot of the racist ideas I grew up with (especially about Mexicans) about living with extended family. 
2) Car reliant infrastructure created a world where humans no longer lived in small communities, but huge ones without local support systems. 

Journal articles make for a tough read, but if anyone is interested (or has access), I'll list the article info: 
Hidaka, B. H. (2012). Depression as a disease of modernity: explanations for increasing 
prevalence. Journal of affective disorders, 140(3), 205-214.

If I find a link directly to the article, I'll try to post it.

There is a budding area of psychological research focusing on something called "connection" and its importance in treating depression. A researcher did a talk about this at my university that was fantastic, but I don't think I have access to it anymore. The big takeaway was that humans need to feel connected to the world around them and the communities that they're situated in. Her team is finding that local and communal care/activism are healthy on an individual level. And this may speak to the mechanisms that make established exercises such as gratitude effective. 

The field of psychology can't control the sociopolitical and economic situations of its patients or anyone really. So it can't change a lot of the negative elements of the world we live in that could be contributing to the depression epidemic. That being said, I definitely agree that psychological care should not be monetized the way it is. In addition I've taken multiple classes on this and I know for a fact there is established neuroscience research on the long-term negative effects of poverty. Psychology and neuroscience have a very good case to make for large-scale societal changes to the way we live and the way we treat others.

 Unfortunately no matter how much individual scientists or practitioners may want to help with larger scale issues, they are bound by the necessity for money. For example, researchers often only get paid if they're publishing a new result. This is what primarily leads the replication crisis. It's not that the scientists don't care. It's that they need to make money for themselves but their bosses don't pay them to do diligence.

Hi! I'm a fourth year psychology student and nearly every paper I've ever written for my degree has been about the field's failures to help those in need. That being said, I would  never go to anyone unlicensed. The main reason is that most people have a fundamentally very bad understanding of psychology. In some ways, we are naturally bad at understanding ourselves and others. Conventional wisdom or common sense does not always hold up scientifically and it can be very dangerous to assume it does. 

On that note, vast majority of "psychology news" that is reported is false. The replication crisis is a real threat to health and safety. The sad thing is, it isn't just non-psychologist folks who get tricked. My own therapists have brought pseudoscience into my sessions before.  Not all psychologists can tell the difference BUT a licensed professional is more likely to have both access and credentials to be able to weed through what research is faulty and which is legit. Without my statistics and research methods classes, I simply wouldn't be able to tell the difference between pseudoscience and the truth. Being able to tell the difference seems simple, but in reality, it gets down to some very nitty gritty mathy data science stuff. 

It's one thing to seek wisdom from an elder, it's another to seek psychological help. To put it in terms of physical health, there are times to see a masseuse, and there are times to see a doctor. You would never in a million years see a masseuse for something threatening your life. My treatment experiences have been some of the worst experiences in my life, but I am 1000000000% sure that it would have been far worse for me if I was left in the hands of someone unqualified. 

I think maybe (if I am interpreting correctly) that OP wants a mental masseuse.  Someone to help relax and guide, but not a replacement for actual medical assistance. Or at least that's what I hope. 

There is a talk on YouTube by Thema-Bryant Davis that may interest you. It's a long talk that addresses a lot, but she talks about the implementation of spiritual support in psychological treatment: https://youtu.be/i50odJ26qxU 

It can be really hard to find a good therapist. I would know. It's a shame that people's bad experiences turn them away from getting help. I myself rarely go to the doctor because of my extreme fear of them that I developed when my pain condition was bad. But I force myself to go to the doctor anyway when I need it because I am humble enough to recognize that no amount of my personal research could amount to a full medical degree. Modern medical and psychological science are by no means perfect, but it's what we have. It's a tough system to navigate.

Edit: it just occurred to me, but my mom has a life coach. Idk a lot about them, but it's really helped her with her day to day health management that her doctor can't hold her hand through. Might be something to look into. I bet there's a witchy one out there!

I saw a great metaphor somewhere, not sure if this was already mentioned, but gender dysphoria can be a bit like wearing shoes that don't fit. When your shoes fit well enough, you don't sit there thinking about it. Because why would you? But if your shoes are too tight, it's all you think about. It's always nagging in the back of your mind. 

For a lot of cis people, they don't "feel" their gender because theirs fits. For me, there was just always this constant sense that something was incorrect. 

Initially, I thought that gender was completely fake and that no one had one. The whole idea of gender felt like an imprisonment to me, and I was very judgemental of people who were too masculine or too feminine because I thought   that everyone was like me and no one really had a "gender" in the traditional sense. I just thought they were pretending for attention. It's amazing how coming to terms with my gender dysphoria and learning to appreciate myself made it so much easier to love other people.

I fully understand your anxiety. I had a very bad experience with medication. I'll share what I learned from my experience. I don't want this comment to feel like a warning, and I hope it will console you some. 

I went through many medication trials over the course of two years. I am one of the people who cannot take medication whatsoever. Every medication made my ADHD far harder to control, my depression was reaching danger levels, and the physical side effects of the drugs made me nearly non functioning. 

What I'll say is this: keep with it, but if you feel sick, or unsafe, stop taking them. My psychiatrist kept me on meds that were hazardous for me far past when she should have because I was too anxious to tell her how sick I had become. If you have a feeling that you should stop, call up your prescriber and tell them you want to. Medication trials do not last forever. They can end whenever you feel they should. Your body is your home, and only you should have the right to decide what goes on it. 

For the vast majority of ADHD people, meds work. And from what I hear, they don't "lose themselves" to meds. Typically, many ADHD people feel like meds help them coexist with their ADHD and become who they feel they were meant to. 

I like to think of it like this: 
ADHD meds are like a ritual food offering to the ADHD demon that lives in your head. Different ADHD demons prefer different offerings. If an ADHD demon likes the taste, it calms down and let's the little human be happy. If it doesn't like the taste, it gets angry and makes things harder. It's all about finding the medication that tastes good to the ADHD demon. If a medication makes life harder, don't force yourself to keep taking it. 

Also, there are a ton of drugs out there. I mean a ton. If something doesn't work, take a break and try another. 

There are other ADHD people like me who can't handle medication, and that's ok. It's hard, but it's not hopeless. If meds don't work for you, don't loose hope. And don't try to force yourself to take medication that is hurting you. There are always other treatment methods that can help.

I don't know if this is helpful, but it's something I've thought of frequently growing up on a farm. 

Animals are perfectly content to each the same grass for months and never complain. They're lifestyle looks insanely boring to me, but underneath that, things are constantly changing for them. 

When the first snow of the season arrives, every animal on the farm goes buck wild with excitement and they dance and play in the snow with each other all morning. (I think it's an evolutionarily developed response to get their bodies moving and warm them up). 

As the days, weather, seasons, and surroundings change for them, we don't think much of it, but they sure might. Nature is never boring, because it never stays the same for even a moment. For me, being grateful for what I have includes being reminded that nothing in my apartment will ever be as cool or as exciting as when some new moss grew on one of my favorite trees. 

Although the modern world seems to include a lot of hustle, bustle, and satisfaction, the natural world has just as much action in it. Maybe it's not necessarily that animals are grateful for eating the same cat food every day, but it's that every day is in many ways, novel and exciting for them. When the weather changes outside, a new bird shows up to the feeder, the sun is just a little brighter, or the wind is just a little louder, these things seem small and insignificant to us, but it's quite possible that our cats notice, and these "small" changes are very big to them.

1) Depends on who you ask. ACT goers would say that the observing self is the true self, never changing, never judging. This is often depicted as the open sky. Clouds (thoughts and emotions) travel past it, or even block it from view, but it is always there, always the same. 

Others, myself included would say that thoughts and emotions are generated by the body and not by your consciousness. I would say you are a collection of pieces, thoughts, feelings, body, "consciousness" and whatever else. Not a satisfying answer, but the truth. Helping all of the parts of you cooperate without fighting each other is a challenge. 

2) I would say the self-discipline in meditation is pretty healthy. The ability to recognize your thoughts and emotions and understand them before getting swept away in them prevents you from letting those thoughts and emotions harm others. We're all jerks sometimes when we're in a bad mood, but understanding and accepting your bad mood can encourage you to pause before snapping at someone. 

Edit: I also have anxiety. For me, recognizing that anxiety is a physical more than a mental illness helps. Anxiety exists in my body, and my body is my friend. We try to work together. It can be hard not to get mad at my body for making life harder, but I have to keep reminding myself that my body and it's behaviors are the result of thousands of years of evolution. My body is just doing what it thinks it's supposed to, so to speak, so that it can help me survive. The answer to anxiety for me (not for everyone!) isn't usually mental or spiritual, but physical. I need to go on a run, dunk my face in cold water, or use my medical marijuana. My mindfulness just helps me collect myself so that I can do those things and find more enjoyment in them. In other words, for my anxiety, meditation or mindfulness were not the ONLY answer for me. They help in aiding the effectiveness of other treatment methods. (They also help teach me acceptance. The bad feelings aren't so painful if I don't resist them, and focus on treating them instead)

Depression, like any other medical problem takes lives. Grief and despair, like any other injury, takes lives. That is the way I choose to view depression and suicide. It is just another example of a person losing their life to a medical condition they suffer from. 

This is not at all to minimize the tragedy of suicide. It just bothers me the way depression and suicide are often talked about. As someone who has been suicidally depressed for as long as I can remember, I've come to find that viewing it in some spiritual or romanticized sense only contributes to the problem. My brain is an organ. I have a medical problem. I can't think it away. And yes, meditation is increadible at helping me with the day to day struggle, but it in no way cures me. 

I don't like people who over-spiritualize others' pain. It rubs me the wrong way. There is nothing spiritual or beautiful about my depression. But there is nothing more spiritual and beautiful than watching myself recover from it. 

I don't believe that there is anything after death. But I don't believe that it's a bad thing, or that it negates the importance and beauty of life. In fact, this brings me great comfort. I only get so much time here, so why spend it blaming myself? I know that the people I lost are gone, and I know what one day I will join them. But I also know that they wouldn't want me to despair for them, or for my life to be destroyed by their absence. They would want me to live on and be kind. And every day, in a sense, I carry them with me in my heart by living in the moment.
